title: There are wounds that come from enemies…
paragraphs: There are wounds that come from enemies…
…and then there are wounds that come from someone who once sat at your table.

He knew what it felt like to dodge spears from Saul.
He knew what it felt like to flee from armies.
He knew what it felt like to survive war, bloodshed, humiliation, caves, betrayal, and public shame.
But there was one betrayal that struck deeper than all the others.
Not because it came from a battlefield…
From someone who knew his private thoughts.
Most people read his name quickly and move on.
Because some betrayals do not just break your circumstances.
They break your ability to breathe normally.

They shake your memory.
Your trust.
Your sleep.
Your appetite.
Your confidence.
Your sense of safety.
Especially when the betrayal comes from someone who once knew your soul.
The story begins quietly in the shadows of David’s collapse.

His son Absalom was orchestrating rebellion against him.
The kingdom was fracturing.
Whispers were spreading through Israel.
Loyalty was shifting.
And then Scripture drops one devastating sentence.
“Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.”
That single line carried enough weight to crush a king.
Because Ahithophel was not just another advisor.
“Now the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counseled in those days, was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God.”
“As if one had asked at the word of God.”
People treated Ahithophel’s wisdom like divine guidance itself.
This was the man David listened to when the pressure was unbearable.
The man who knew strategies nobody else knew.
The man who understood David’s weaknesses, fears, and patterns.

The person you defended.
The person you opened your life to.
The person who sat beside you during victories…
now standing beside the people trying to destroy you.
Some of you know this pain too well.

But the person who shattered you…
was someone you loved.
Someone who knew exactly where to place the knife.
That is why Psalm 55 feels less like poetry…

But it is you,
a man my equal,
my companion,
my familiar friend.”
The Hebrew wording here is emotionally devastating.
Close enough to wound me personally.
“We used to take sweet counsel together.”
The phrase “sweet counsel” comes from the Hebrew:
David is describing someone who once walked beside him in worship…
and later helped orchestrate his destruction.
Some scholars strongly believe Psalm 55 was written directly about Ahithophel.
And suddenly the pain becomes horrifyingly human.
but betrayal from intimacy dismantles you.
And here is where the story becomes even darker.
Ahithophel did not merely betray David politically.
There may have been something deeply personal underneath it.
In 2 Samuel 23:34, Ahithophel is identified as the father of Eliam.
Eliam was the father of Bathsheba.
That means Ahithophel may have been Bathsheba’s grandfather.
Let that settle into your chest for a moment.

David slept with Bathsheba.
David orchestrated Uriah’s death.
David shattered a family.
Ahithophel may have carried silent bitterness that eventually exploded into rebellion.
Because sometimes betrayal is born from unresolved wounds.
Sometimes people smile while secretly nursing years of pain.
Sometimes the people closest to you are silently bleeding because of decisions you made long ago.
but forgiveness does not erase earthly consequences.
But sin still leaves scars across relationships.
This is one of the most sobering truths in all Scripture.
and still watch certain consequences unfold painfully.
“Whatever one sows, that will he also reap.”
and years later watched devastation grow publicly.

Absalom’s rebellion.
Division.
Humiliation.
And Ahithophel’s betrayal.
This is why secret compromise is so dangerous.
Because what begins in hidden rooms eventually reaches entire generations.
the story becomes even more heartbreaking.
When Ahithophel realized his counsel would not be followed, he went home, put his affairs in order…
The same kind of despair later associated with Judas.
Both close enough to sacred spaces to hear truth regularly.
Both ending in despair instead of repentance.
And suddenly Ahithophel no longer feels like merely a villain.
A man whose wisdom could not save his own soul.
And this is where the article turns directly toward us.
Because many people today are carrying Ahithophel hearts.
Following Jesus externally while internally feeding resentment.
Bitterness is dangerous because it disguises itself as justified pain.
“See to it that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble.”
The Greek word for bitterness is:

It leaks into conversations.
Relationships.
Thoughts.
Decisions.
Families.
Churches.
it destroys the person carrying it.
That is exactly what happened to Ahithophel.
Some of you reading this have been betrayed deeply.
And the terrifying temptation is becoming what wounded you.
And if surrendered to darkness long enough, pain starts teaching revenge.
This is why Christ’s betrayal matters so much.
Because Jesus also knew what it felt like to be betrayed by intimacy.
Judas did not betray Him from a distant mountain.
He betrayed Him after eating with Him.

“Even my close friend in whom I trusted,
who ate my bread,
has lifted his heel against me.”
The Hebrew phrase “lifted his heel” paints the image of violent rejection.

Release.
Send away.
Cancel the debt.
But refusing to let betrayal become your identity.
Some people reading this are still emotionally trapped inside what somebody did to you years ago.
Still carrying names in your chest that tighten your throat when remembered.
But bitterness will never resurrect your peace.
Only Christ can heal wounds this deep.
The same David who was betrayed…
later wrote some of the most honest cries ever recorded in Scripture.
Because broken people who run toward God instead of away from Him become living evidence of grace.
But Jesus entered human betrayal and conquered sin itself.
And maybe this article found you at the exact right moment.
Maybe you are the betrayed one.
you became Ahithophel without realizing it.
Maybe resentment has been growing silently inside you for years.
Maybe offense has been discipling your heart more than Scripture.
Maybe your smile hides exhaustion, anger, envy, disappointment, or unforgiveness.
But Jesus is still calling people out of darkness.
And no betrayal is deeper than the mercy of God.

Be honest.
This hit some wounds you thought were buried.

Some betrayals do not just break your heart…
they reveal who is truly ruling it.
